claims.text: A machine-learning model combining image-based microstructural descriptors with physics-based simulation outputs can predict Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture behavior of hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10.
The as-reported HfNbTiVAl10 alloy exhibits a hierarchical heterostructure.
Fractal dimensions, spatial correlation functions, and local phase-connectivity metrics can quantitatively represent the relevant hierarchy in HfNbTiVAl10.
Gradient boosting is a suitable ensemble method for the proposed regression framework.
The proposed framework will fuse descriptors from high-resolution images with outputs from a limited number of physics-based simulations.
The prediction scope is tensile and fracture testing at ambient or application-relevant temperatures and strain rates while the hierarchical microstructure remains preserved.
The HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure includes nanoprecipitates, multiscale phase connectivity, and spatial correlations.
These hierarchical features govern local stress distribution and deformation initiation in HfNbTiVAl10.
Combining microstructural information with physics-based features can capture factors influencing mechanical properties more effectively than composition-only representations.
A trained surrogate model can avoid repeated computationally intensive full-scale calculations and make prediction easier or faster.
The proposed model will be approximately an order of magnitude faster than established simulations.
The proposed model will reduce prediction error by approximately 10–15% relative to established simulation methods.
The claimed accuracy improvement or comparability applies jointly to Young’s modulus, yield strength, and fracture characteristics.
Atomistic and other physically based simulations can require lengthy calculations and substantial computational resources.
Traditional continuum or atomistic simulations struggle to resolve the multiscale effects in the hierarchical HfNbTiVAl10 heterostructure.
Prediction performance may deteriorate at extreme strain rates, high temperatures, or after processing variations when the microstructure changes outside the descriptor domain.
Insufficient, low-quality, or unrepresentative training data may cause the machine-learning approach to fail.
Young’s modulus can be obtained from the elastic stress–strain response, and yield strength can be determined using a 0.2% offset.
Digital image correlation can provide the stated fracture-toughness and crack-initiation or propagation measurements for the proposed decisive test.

The hypothesis will be declared falsified if model predictions consistently differ by more than approximately 15% from independent measurements for any targeted property across multiple specimens and conditions.
